sampling-dist-proportion-s1.title: Testing a seed company's sprouting rate
sampling-dist-proportion-s1.text: A seed company says that 85% of its tomato seeds sprout. A garden store plants a random sample of 200 seeds from a shipment of 50,000 seeds and records the proportion that sprout. Suppose the company's figure is correct, so $p = 0.85$.

table.caption: The setting for the sampling distribution of the sample proportion

sampling-dist-proportion-s2.title: Left-handed students in samples of 30
sampling-dist-proportion-s2.text: A school has 900 students, and 90 of them (10%) are left-handed. A computer takes 200 random samples of 30 students, without replacement, and records the proportion of left-handed students in each sample.

plot.label: Histogram of 200 simulated sample proportions of left-handed students, samples of 30, skewed right with a peak near 0.07 to 0.10

items.q: What are the mean and standard deviation of the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$, the proportion of the 200 seeds that sprout?
options: Mean 0.85, standard deviation 0.0252
Mean 0.85, standard deviation 0.000638
Mean 0.85, standard deviation 0.357
Mean 170, standard deviation 5.05
Right: the mean is $p$ and the standard deviation is $\sqrt{p(1 - p)/n}$.
That is $\frac{p(1 - p)}{n}$ without the square root: the variance, not the standard deviation.
That is $\sqrt{p(1 - p)}$, the spread for a single seed. Divide by $n$ inside the square root.
Those describe the count of seeds that sprout, $np$ and $\sqrt{np(1 - p)}$, not the proportion.

items.q: Calculate the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$. Give four decimal places.

mistakes.why: That is $\frac{p(1 - p)}{n}$, the variance. Take its square root to get the standard deviation.
That is $\sqrt{p(1 - p)}$, with no division by $n$. Divide $p(1 - p)$ by the sample size before taking the square root.
That is $\sqrt{np(1 - p)}$, the standard deviation of the count of seeds that sprout. For the proportion, divide by $n$ inside the square root.

why.correct: $\sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1 - p)}{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.85(0.15)}{200}} = \sqrt{0.0006375} = 0.0252$. The 10% condition holds (200 is less than 10% of 50,000), so this formula applies.

items.q: Why is it reasonable to use a normal model for the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$ here?
options: Because $n = 200$ is at least 30
Because 200 is less than 10% of the 50,000 seeds in the shipment
Because the seeds were chosen at random

why.correct: The large counts condition: $np = 200(0.85) = 170$ and $n(1 - p) = 200(0.15) = 30$ are both at least 10, so the distribution of $\hat{p}$ is approximately normal.
options: The rule of 30 is for sample means. For proportions, check the expected numbers of successes and failures.
That is the 10% condition. It justifies the standard deviation formula, not the normal shape.
Right: the large counts condition, with both counts at least 10.
Random selection is needed, but it does not make the shape normal. The shape depends on the expected numbers of successes and failures.

items.q: Assuming the company's figure is correct, find the probability that 80% or fewer of the 200 seeds sprout.

mistakes.why: That is $P(\hat{p} \ge 0.80)$, the area above 0.80. "80% or fewer" is the area below.
That uses 0.80 in the standard deviation. The sampling distribution is built from the true $p = 0.85$: $\sqrt{0.85(0.15)/200}$.
That uses a standard deviation of 0.0357 or similar. Check the formula: $\sqrt{p(1 - p)/n} = 0.0252$.

why.correct: $\hat{p}$ is approximately normal with mean 0.85 and standard deviation 0.0252. $z = \frac{0.80 - 0.85}{0.0252} = -1.98$, so $P(\hat{p} \le 0.80) = P(Z \le -1.98) = 0.024$. Technology (normal, mean 0.85, SD 0.0252, below 0.80) gives 0.0239.

items.q: Type the expression for the z-score of $\hat{p} = 0.80$ in this sampling distribution, with the values substituted (as you would show it on the exam).

mistakes.why: The standard deviation of $\hat{p}$ uses the true $p = 0.85$, not the value 0.80 you are standardizing.
The standard deviation needs a square root: $\sqrt{0.85(0.15)/200}$.
Subtract in the order value minus mean, so a value below the mean gets a negative z-score.

why.correct: Standardize: $z = \frac{\hat{p} - p}{\sqrt{p(1 - p)/n}} = \frac{0.80 - 0.85}{\sqrt{0.85(0.15)/200}} = -1.98$. The standard deviation uses the true $p = 0.85$.

items.q: Why is the simulated sampling distribution skewed right instead of approximately normal?
options: Because $np = 30(0.10) = 3$ is less than 10
Because 200 samples is too few to show the true shape
Because 30 is more than 10% of the school
Because the samples were taken without replacement

why.correct: With $n = 30$ and $p = 0.10$, the expected number of left-handed students is $np = 3$, less than 10. The proportion cannot go below 0 but can go well above 0.10, so the distribution is skewed right.
options: Right: the large counts condition fails for successes.
More simulated samples would show the same skewed shape more smoothly; the shape comes from $n$ and $p$.
10% of 900 is 90, and 30 is less than that, so the 10% condition holds.
Sampling without replacement is fine when the sample is under 10% of the population; it does not cause the skew.

items.q: Calculate the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample proportion for samples of 30 from this school. Give four decimal places.

mistakes.why: That is $\frac{p(1 - p)}{n}$, the variance. Take the square root.
That is $\sqrt{p(1 - p)}$, with no division by the sample size inside the square root.

why.correct: The 10% condition holds ($30 \le 90$), so $\sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.10(0.90)}{30}} = 0.0548$. The simulated proportions have a standard deviation close to this.

items.q: What is the smallest sample size for which the large counts condition holds with $p = 0.10$?

why.correct: Large counts needs $np \ge 10$ and $n(1 - p) \ge 10$. With $p = 0.10$, $0.10n \ge 10$ gives $n \ge 100$; then $n(0.90) = 90$ is also at least 10.
options: At $n = 30$, $np = 3$: the condition fails, as the skewed histogram shows.
$n = 300$ meets the condition, but so do smaller samples; the smallest is 100.
$90(0.10) = 9$, just short of 10.

items.q: To meet the large counts condition, the computer takes samples of 100 from this school of 900. Which condition is now a problem, and what does it affect?
options: Large counts: the shape of the distribution is still skewed right with samples of 100
The 10% condition: the standard deviation formula overstates the spread
Random: samples of 100 are not random
The 10% condition: the mean is no longer equal to $p$

why.correct: 10% of 900 is 90, and 100 is more than that. When a sample is more than 10% of the population, draws without replacement are not close to independent, so $\sqrt{p(1 - p)/n}$ overstates the spread of $\hat{p}$.
options: With $n = 100$, $np = 10$ and $n(1 - p) = 90$, so large counts now holds.
Right: 100 is more than 90, 10% of the school, so the formula is no longer accurate.
The computer still selects at random; the issue is how large the sample is compared with the school.
The mean of $\hat{p}$ is still $p$ for random samples. What the 10% condition protects is the standard deviation formula.

items.q: A pollster keeps everything else the same but takes a random sample 4 times as large. By what factor does the standard deviation of $\hat{p}$ change?
options: It is divided by 4
It is divided by 2
It is multiplied by 2
It does not change, because $p$ is the same

why.correct: $\sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1 - p)}{n}}$ has $n$ under a square root. Replacing $n$ with $4n$ divides it by $\sqrt{4} = 2$.
options: The sample size is inside a square root, so the effect is $\sqrt{4}$, not 4.
Right: $\sqrt{4n}$ is twice $\sqrt{n}$.
A larger sample gives less spread, not more.
The formula depends on $n$ as well as $p$.

items.q: In a large city, 50% of voters favor a new transit tax. A random sample of 400 voters is taken. Find the probability that 55% or more of the sample favors the tax.

mistakes.why: That is the area below 0.55. "55% or more" is the area above.
That comes from a standard deviation of $\frac{0.5(0.5)}{400}$ with no square root, which makes $z$ enormous. Take the square root: 0.025.

items.q: A researcher selects 120 nurses at random, without replacement, from a hospital system with 6,000 nurses. Which condition makes it reasonable to treat the 120 selections as independent?
options: The large counts condition
The 10% condition: 120 is less than 600
Random selection of the 120 nurses from the full list
A sample size of at least 30

why.correct: When a sample is no more than 10% of the population, selections without replacement are close enough to independent. 120 is less than 10% of 6,000, which is 600.
options: Large counts is about the shape of the sampling distribution, not independence.
Right: the sample is less than 10% of the population.
Random selection avoids bias. It does not by itself make draws without replacement independent.
That rule of thumb is about sample means and shape, not independence.

items.q: About 3% of a factory's light bulbs are defective. An inspector takes a random sample of 250 bulbs from a large batch. What can you say about the shape of the sampling distribution of the proportion defective?
options: Approximately normal, because 250 is a large sample
Skewed left, because most bulbs are not defective
Approximately normal, because $n(1 - p) = 242.5$
Skewed right, because $250(0.03) = 7.5$ is less than 10

why.correct: $np = 250(0.03) = 7.5$, which is less than 10. Large counts fails, so the distribution is skewed right (it piles up near 0 and has a longer tail to the right).
options: Size alone is not enough: the expected number of defective bulbs is only 7.5.
With $p$ near 0, the proportion piles up near 0 and stretches to the right: skewed right.
Both counts must be at least 10, and $np = 7.5$ is not.
Right: large counts fails for the defective bulbs.

items.q: Which statements about $\sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1 - p)}{n}}$ are true? Select all that apply.
options: It gets smaller as the sample size increases
For a fixed sample size, it is largest when $p = 0.5$
Doubling the sample size cuts it in half
It is larger for a population of 10 million than for one of 100,000

why.correct: The standard deviation shrinks as $n$ grows, and for a fixed $n$, $p(1 - p)$ is largest at $p = 0.5$. It shrinks with the square root of $n$, so doubling $n$ divides it by about 1.41, not 2.
options: Right: $n$ is in the denominator.
Right: $p(1 - p)$ peaks at $0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25$.
Doubling $n$ divides it by $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41$; it takes 4 times the sample size to halve it.
As long as the sample is under 10% of the population, the population size does not appear in the formula.

items.q: A random sample of 100 adults is replaced by a random sample of 900 adults from the same large population. What happens to the mean of the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$?
options: It moves closer to $p$
It is divided by 3
It stays equal to $p$
It becomes 9 times as large

why.correct: $\mu_{\hat{p}} = p$ for any sample size: the sample proportion is an unbiased estimator. The sample size changes only the spread.
options: It already equals $p$ at any sample size.
The mean does not depend on $n$; the standard deviation is the part that is divided by $\sqrt{9} = 3$.
Right: the center is $p$ whatever the sample size.
That would describe the mean count of successes, $np$, not the proportion.

items.q: The garden store plants a random sample of 200 seeds and only 78% sprout. Assuming 85% of all the company's seeds sprout, $P(\hat{p} \le 0.78) = 0.0028$. Build a sentence that uses this probability to judge the company's claim.

options: Assuming 85% of all the company's seeds sprout
Assuming 78% of all the company's seeds sprout
Assuming 85% of these 200 seeds sprout

why.1: The probability was computed assuming the company's 85%, not the sample's 78%.
why.2: The assumption is about all the company's seeds, the population, not this sample.

options: a sample proportion of 0.78 or less would be very unusual (probability 0.0028)
a sample proportion of 0.78 or less would be quite likely (probability 0.0028)
there is a 0.0028 probability that the company is right

why.1: A probability of 0.0028 is very small: about 3 times in 1,000 samples.
why.2: The probability assumes the claim is true; it is not the probability that the claim is true.

options: so this result gives reason to doubt the company's claim
so this result shows the claim is false
so this result supports the company's claim

why.1: An unusual result casts doubt on a claim; it does not show the claim is false for certain.
why.2: An outcome this unlikely under the claim counts against the claim, not for it.

conclude.model: Assuming 85% of all the company's seeds sprout, a sample proportion of 0.78 or less in a random sample of 200 seeds would be very unusual (probability 0.0028), so this result gives reason to doubt the company's claim.

why.correct: A probability is useful only when you tie it back to the claim. If the claim were true, 78% or fewer sprouting would happen in about 3 of every 1,000 samples, so it would be very unusual. That casts doubt on the claim.
